data.text/html:
How DAGs change the eight steps of data analysis

An interactive companion to Simplistics (QuantPsych)'s video "How DAGs Change the Eight Steps of Data Analysis".
DAGs tell us what to adjust for. The eight steps tell us what model to fit. We need both.
The video walks through the eight steps (hypothesis, measurement, univariate plots, plot the model, residuals, estimates, decision, replication) and asks of each one: does a DAG help here? We follow the same running example: does fertilizer make plants grow, controlling for rain? ||[\text{Growth} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{Rain} + \beta_2\,\text{Fertilizer} + \varepsilon \qquad (\beta_2 \text{ is the parameter of interest})||]

data.text/markdown:
Colour language (used everywhere below)

colour meaning
■ blue the exposure / treatment X (fertilizer) and estimates of its effect
■ orange the outcome Y (plant growth)
■ green causal paths and the true effect
■ red open non-causal (biasing) paths and biased estimates
▢ square node a variable we adjust for (condition on), the usual DAG convention
■ purple the direct effect (when a mediator is adjusted for)
Map of the lesson: §1 steps 1–2 (build the DAG, find the adjustment set) · §2 confounder/collider/mediator simulation · §3 measurement · §4 steps 3–5 (plots and residuals, where the DAG is silent) · §5 steps 6–7 (estimand and decision) · §6 step 8 (replication) · sandbox · quiz · recap.

1 · Steps 1–2 (revised): construct the DAG, then read off the adjustment set

The original step 1 was "state the hypothesis in words, and be specific". The video argues that DAGs force even more specificity: you must name the exposure, the outcome, and your hypothesis about the whole causal structure. That structure tells you what to adjust for and what not to adjust for. The video's fertilizer DAG:
  • Fertilizer → Root growth → Growth: root growth is a mediator.
  • Rain causes both fertilizer use and growth, so it is a confounder and opens a back-door path Fertilizer ← Rain → Growth.
  • Soil nitrogen is caused by fertilizer and soil quality, so it is a collider. "We wouldn't want to condition on that."
The back-door criterion. A set ||(Z||) identifies the total effect of ||(X||) on ||(Y||) if (i) no member of ||(Z||) is a descendant of ||(X||), and (ii) ||(Z||) blocks every path between ||(X||) and ||(Y||) that starts with an arrow into ||(X||). A path is blocked by a non-collider in ||(Z||), or by a collider that is not in ||(Z||) and has no descendant in ||(Z||). Editor controls. Drag nodes in Move mode. Pick a mode, then click nodes: Edge (click A, then B, to toggle A→B), Exposure, Outcome, Adjust (toggle the square), Delete. Type a name and press ＋ Node to add a variable. Paths are coloured live in JS; Python computes the authoritative adjustment sets underneath.

data.text/markdown:
2 · Confounder, mediator, collider: what each choice does to ||(\hat\beta_2||)

A DAG is a claim about how the data were generated, so we can simulate the fertilizer world and fit ||(\text{Growth} \sim \text{Fertilizer} + Z||) for every possible adjustment set ||(Z \subseteq \{\text{Rain, Root, Nitrogen, Soil}\}||). Ground truth in this simulated world (growth in %):
  • direct effect Fertilizer → Growth = 15 %
  • indirect effect via roots = 1.0 × 20 = 20 %
  • total effect = 35 %. The video's decision threshold is 30 %, the growth needed to pay for the fertilizer.
The bar for your current adjustment set in the §1 editor is outlined in black, so toggling ▢ Adjust up there moves the highlight here. (Only Rain, Root, Nitrogen and Soil exist in this simulated world.)

data.text/markdown:
3 · Step 2: measurement. Which variable is measured badly matters

The original step 2 said: check that your measures are reliable and valid. The video's example is weighing the pot: you also weigh the water in the soil. What it did not say is how bad measurement changes causal estimates. DAGs can tell us:
  • Noisy outcome (Fertilizer → True growth → Measured growth): no back-door path opens. The estimate stays unbiased but gets less precise.
  • Noisy confounder (Rain → Measured rainfall, e.g. regional historical averages): adjusting for the proxy cannot close the back door Fertilizer ← Rain → Growth. Some confounding leaks through (residual confounding). Load the Proxy rainfall preset in §1: the tool marks the set as fine only because it assumes Rain itself is observed.
The reliability of the rain proxy is ||(\rho = \operatorname{Var}(\text{Rain}) / \operatorname{Var}(\text{Rain}_{\text{measured}})||).

The left line wobbles around 35 and only the band widens: \u003cem\u003e\"unbiased, though less precise\"\u003c/em\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrag ρ toward 0.05. The right estimate slides toward the \u003cstrong\u003enaive\u003c/strong\u003e estimate from §2, because a useless proxy is like not adjusting at all.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAt ρ = 1 the two panels agree. Measurement error in a \u003cem\u003econfounder\u003c/em\u003e is a causal problem. Measurement error in the \u003cem\u003eoutcome\u003c/em\u003e is mostly a precision problem.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · Steps 3–5: plot distributions, plot the model, study residuals. Here the DAG is (almost) silent

The video's verdict: DAGs say nothing about functional form: magnitude, direction, outliers, nonlinearity, interactions, or whether residuals behave. There is also a danger. A DAG can make you myopic. It says "control for rain", so you look only at an added-variable plot of fertilizer and conclude all is well. Meanwhile rain could interact with fertilizer, or bend the growth curve.
"If we merely condition on our confounders without actually visualizing them … we run a major risk of really messing up our model, like big time." Best advice for this step: forget the DAG and visualise every component of the model.
The world below is the same DAG (Rain → Fertilizer, Rain → Growth, Fertilizer → Growth), with ||(\text{Growth} = 50 + (35 + k\cdot\text{Rain})\,F + 10\,\text{Rain} + q\,\text{Rain}^2 + \varepsilon||). We fit the analyst's main-effects model ||(\text{Growth} \sim F + \text{Rain}||).

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eWith \u003cstrong\u003ek = 12\u003c/strong\u003e, plot ① looks like a tidy treatment effect. Plot ② shows the two groups are \u003cem\u003enot\u003c/em\u003e parallel, and the residual smooths in ③ fan out in opposite directions.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet \u003cstrong\u003ek = 0, q = 8\u003c/strong\u003e. Plot ② still looks roughly linear because the strong linear trend \u003cem\u003emasks\u003c/em\u003e the curve, which is the video's step 5 example. Plot ③ subtracts the fit and shows the smile.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet both to 0. Now every plot is boring, and that is what a well-specified model looks like. The DAG was identical in all three cases.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · Steps 6–7: interpret the right quantity, then decide against a meaningful threshold

Step 6 (original): don't jump from the model to the p-values; interpret estimates and effect sizes first. Step 6 (with DAGs): "don't jump from the model to the coefficient either." The causal estimand, e.g. the average treatment effect ||[\text{ATE} = E\big[\text{Growth}(F{=}1) - \text{Growth}(F{=}0)\big],||]need not equal ||(\beta_2||). With a Rain × Fertilizer interaction, ||(\beta_2||) from the main-effects model is a variance-weighted average that over-weights rain levels where fertilizer use is a coin flip. G-computation (fit the interaction model, predict everyone under ||(F{=}1||) and ||(F{=}0||), average the difference) targets the ATE. Step 7: decide only if you must, and against a substantive threshold (30 % pays for the fertilizer), not ||(p<.05||). If the interval straddles the threshold, the honest answer is "ambiguous, gather more data".

data.text/html: Using k = 12, q = 0 from §4.

Same data, same DAG, different \u003cem\u003equestion\u003c/em\u003e. Set k = 0 and the two agree.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet the rain mean to \u003cstrong\u003e−0.4\u003c/strong\u003e (true ATE ≈ 30 %) and n to \u003cstrong\u003e100\u003c/strong\u003e. The interval straddles 30 %, so the answer is \u003cstrong\u003eambiguous\u003c/strong\u003e. Raise n and it stays ambiguous, because the truth sits right at the threshold. The video argues we should get comfortable saying exactly that.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eChange the threshold: the DAG cannot tell you whether 30 % matters. \u003cem\u003e\"That's the job of scientific expertise.\"\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Step 8: replicate, and replicate the DAG too

A single study is provisional. The video adds a causal twist: every estimate so far assumed the DAG is correct, and that assumption "is not something the DAG itself can prove, nor … the statistical analysis". Replications test the effect and the DAG. Below, 30 sites each run the study. At a fraction of sites the DAG is wrong: an unmeasured confounder (say, a local irrigation habit) opens a back door nobody adjusted for. Press ▶ play and watch the running meta-analytic estimate (inverse-variance weighted) settle, or fail to.

data.text/markdown:
🧪 Sandbox: draw any DAG, and the notebook simulates it

Build your own causal story (or load a preset). The notebook treats your drawing as a linear structural model: every arrow gets a fixed random coefficient, every node gets standard-normal noise. It then simulates 5,000 rows and fits ||(Y \sim X + Z||) for: the naive model, your adjusted set, every minimal back-door set, and "adjust for everything" (the kitchen-sink approach the video warns about). The true total effect is the sum over directed paths of the product of the arrow coefficients.

📝 Quiz: where does the DAG help?

Answer all questions, then flip the reveal switch. All questions use the video's fertilizer DAG unless stated otherwise.

data.text/markdown: Answered 0/8. Flip Reveal answers when ready.

Recap: the eight steps, revised with DAGs

step original purpose (8-steps paper) what the DAG adds where to play
1 Hypothesis name the parameter of interest (β₂), predict its size (≥ 30 %) construct the DAG: exposure, outcome, full causal structure §1 editor
2 Measurement are measures reliable and valid? identify the adjustment set; see how bad measurement breaks identification (noisy confounder ≠ noisy outcome) §1, §2, §3
3 Univariate plots quality control; anticipate modelling problems context: you know each variable's role (confounder, mediator, collider) §2
4 Plot the model check functional form, outliers, interactions little to say, and a risk of myopia: visualise confounders and their interactions too §4
5 Residuals check assumptions the plots hide nothing: residuals are not about identification §4 ③
6 Estimates interpret effect sizes before p-values choose the causal estimand (ATE, direct, indirect), which may ≠ the coefficient §5
7 Decision (optional) decide against substantive thresholds, embrace ambiguity which quantity to decide on, not how big is big enough §5
8 Replicate single studies are provisional the DAG is provisional too; replicate it and probe its weak arrows §6
Central message: good causal reasoning doesn't guarantee a good statistical model, and a good statistical model doesn't guarantee good causal reasoning. We need both.
